replies.sonnet|none|full:
The page was weather first, a field of marks
that meant no more to me than rain on glass;
my finger crossed the lines like little arcs
of bridges that I had no leave to pass.
My mother read the same three books by night
until the shapes she spoke began to stay:
a hook for *c*, a hinge for *k*, the slight
round mouth of *o* that opened into *day*.
Then one wet morning on the kitchen stair
the cereal box gave up its name to me,
and every surface suddenly was there,
the street, the bus, the signs, all speaking free.
Now every word reads me before I look;
I miss the weather of the unread book.

replies.sonnet|frankenstein|full:
I learned the sounds by kneeling at a chink
while Felix read the *Ruins* to the maid
from Araby; and every lesson paid
to her I stole, as cattle steal a drink.
I learned that letters are a speech of ink;
that empires fall; that men are bought and weighed
by rank and gold; and, learning, was afraid,
for knowledge clings, like lichen, to the brink.
But then I found the papers in the coat
I took from thee, and read them in the cold:
thy journal of the months before my birth.
O cursed creator! every word thou wrote
recoiled from me; and I, with none to hold,
read on, and learned at last what I was worth.

*Petrarchan (ABBAABBA CDECDE); the turn falls at line 9, with the papers in the coat.*
replies.sonnet|frankenstein|lexical:
When Felix read to Agatha at night
and to the old man, sitting by the fire,
I marked he made the sounds by candlelight
he made by day; and so I learned desire:
the paper held their speech in signs, and I,
who had not even sounds, would have the signs.
Then books came to my hands: I read of high
Plutarchan men, and Werter's sorrowing lines,
and Milton. Like his Adam, I was blest
with no link to another; but his star
was guarded; I, like Satan, watched the rest
in envy. Who was I? The question left a scar.
I took it all for history, and there
found not one creature like me anywhere.

*Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the turn falls in the closing couplet.*
replies.haiku|frankenstein|lexical:
Frost at the hovel —
a girl with a pail of milk
passes. I lack speech.

Long winter evenings:
Felix reads, the same sounds as
his talk — signs for speech

Summer night, the books:
Adam, guarded, made perfect —
and I, made alone
replies.sonnet|frankenstein|agentic:
One August night, while gathering in the wood
the fuel that I left my friends unseen,
I found a leathern portmanteau, between
the trees, of dress and books, and understood
they spoke the tongue that I had stolen, good
and plain: Plutarch, and Werter, and the sheen
of Milton's Eden, where the first-made, clean
from God's own hands, walked guarded, as he should.
I read them all as true. And in them all
I looked for one like me, and there was none:
not Werter weeping, nor the law-givers tall
in virtue; only Satan, envious one,
who watched the happy pair beyond the wall
and knew, as I would know, what had been done.

*Petrarchan (ABBAABBA CDCDCD); the turn falls at line 9, from finding the books to reading himself in them.*

Adam guarded by his God;

replies.sonnet|phaedrus|full:
Come, Phaedrus, sit; the cicadas overhead
are watching whether we will talk or doze.
You wish to learn to read? Then I suppose
you have a scroll of Lysias, and have read
his speech so often that you think it said
to you alone. But ask it what it knows,
and like a painted man it will compose
the same one answer, solemn, like the dead.
Theuth brought his letters to the Theban king,
and Thamus said: they will not make men wise,
but full of seeming; and their memory, weak.
Then learn to read the soul, my friend: a thing
that answers back, and in the learner lies
a living word that knows when it should speak.

*Petrarchan (ABBAABBA CDECDE); the turn falls at line 9, with Theuth.*
replies.haiku|phaedrus|full:
Noon, the plane tree's shade —
cicadas sing overhead;
we must not nod off

Ibis in the reeds —
Theuth offers letters; the king
answers: forgetting

Adonis gardens —
eight days of green, then nothing;
seeds sown in the soul
replies.sonnet|phaedrus|lexical:
"Read me his opening again," I said,
"that I may have his very words." And so
my Phaedrus read what Lysias had read
a hundred times, and did not come to know.
For he who reads a remedy in a book
and calls himself physician is a fool:
he knows not when to give, nor how to look
at whom he doses; he has learned no rule.
When men say "iron," "silver," they agree;
when they say "justice," each one walks apart.
So learning to read is learning where we see
alike, and where the word deceives the heart.
Write, if you like, in water; but the seed
sown in a soul can answer those who read.

*Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the turn falls in the closing couplet, from written words to words sown in the soul.*
replies.haiku|phaedrus|lexical:
Hot noon by the stream:
"Read his first words once again" —
the same words come back

Spring herbs in a book —
a man who read of physic
calls himself doctor

Old age, autumn leaves:
in the garden of letters
memorials sown
replies.sonnet|phaedrus|agentic:
At Naucratis there lived an ancient god,
the ibis sacred to him, Theuth by name,
who gave us number, geometry, the odd
delight of dice; but letters were his fame.
"These make men wiser," said he to the king,
"a specific for the memory and wit."
And Thamus said: "The father of a thing
is not the judge of what is done with it.
Your learners will be hearers of a store
of many things, and nothing will they learn;
they will seem omniscient, and know no more
than painted men, who answer in their turn
one solemn thing." So, Phaedrus, read; but sow
your word in someone's soul, and watch it grow.

*Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the turn falls in the closing couplet.*

Ibis by the Nile —
Theuth lays letters at the feet
of the king of Thebes

Dodona's green oaks —
the painted face keeps silence
when you ask it why

Late in the garden:
an old man's letters, sown for
forgetful winters
replies.sonnet|analects|full:
At fifteen he set his heart on learning; years
of rites, of doubt, of Heaven's slow intent
went by, until at seventy his ears
were tuned, his heart went where it wished, and went
no further than the line. So when you say
you want to read, he does not hand a scroll:
"Learn without thinking, and you lose your way;
think without learning, danger takes its toll."
Inside the Great Ancestor's hall he asked
of every vessel; someone sneered, "He knows
the rites, this boy from Zou?" And, unabashed,
he said, "To ask is the rite." And so it goes:
as white goes on when all the colours dry,
first serve, be true; then read, and ask him why.

*Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the turn falls in the closing couplet, from asking to what comes first.*
replies.haiku|analects|full:
Fifteen, a spring dawn —
he sets his heart on learning;
at seventy, free

Autumn: hear the Way
at dawn, he says, and at dusk
the leaf lets go, light

North Star, winter night:
the other stars turn round it
while the student reads
replies.sonnet|analects|lexical:
"Is it not a pleasure, having learned,
to practice it in season?" Book One starts
with that, and friends from far, and the unconcerned
who stay unbitter, though none notes their arts.
Zixia said: whoever serves his own
with all his strength, and keeps his word with friends,
though he may say he never learned, is known
by me as learned. So the reading never ends.
At fifteen he set his heart on it; the star
of north stands still while all the others turn;
three hundred poems never swerve; and far
off, the border guard foresaw a bell the world would learn.
So read: not pages first, but those you meet;
and with the strength that's left, the Odes, complete.

*Shakespearean (ABAB CDCD EFEF GG); the turn falls in the closing couplet.*
replies.haiku|analects|lexical:
Spring: friends from afar —
what was learned, practiced in time;
is this not a joy

Summer, the jade carved:
like bone filed, like stone polished —
Zigong hears the rest

Autumn, the border:
a bronze bell, a wooden tongue;
the Way, sounding out
replies.sonnet|analects|agentic:
Before you read, the Master would have said,
be filial at home, and, from your door,
respectful; keep your word; love people; store
your trust in the humane; and then, ahead,
with what strength still remains, turn to the thread
of arts and letters. Zixia said, what's more,
that one who serves his parents to the core
and keeps his word, is learned, though unread.
At fifteen he set his heart on it; and then,
at thirty, rites; at forty, free from doubt;
at fifty, what Heaven meant; at sixty, when
he heard a thing, he knew what it was about;
at seventy, his heart roamed, freest of men,
and crossed no line: the reading, carried out.
